title: Word Pattern Bijection
description:
# Word Pattern Bijection

Given a pattern string `pattern` and a space-separated sentence `s`, determine whether the words in `s` follow the same pattern.

Following the pattern means there is a one-to-one mapping between pattern characters and words:

* each pattern character always maps to the same word;
* no two different pattern characters map to the same word;
* the number of pattern characters must equal the number of words.

Comparisons are case-sensitive, so `Dog` and `dog` are different words.

## Example 1:

**Input:** pattern = "abba", s = "dog cat cat dog"
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** `a` maps to `dog`, and `b` maps to `cat`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** pattern = "abba", s = "dog cat cat fish"
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The character `a` would need to map to both `dog` and `fish`.

## Example 3:

**Input:** pattern = "abba", s = "dog dog dog dog"
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The characters `a` and `b` would both map to `dog`, which violates the one-to-one rule.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= pattern.length <= 300`
*   `s` contains one or more words separated by single spaces.
*   Words and pattern characters are compared case-sensitively.

tests.description: sample with a valid two-way mapping
same pattern letter maps to two different words
one pattern letter cannot map to multiple words
two pattern letters cannot map to the same word
pattern has more characters than words
sentence has more words than pattern characters

tests.input: pattern = "abcabc", s = "red blue green red blue green"
tests.description: mapping must stay consistent across repeated groups
same pattern letter can consistently map to lowercase dog
final a cannot change from dog to Dog

solutions.name: Two Directional Maps
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split the sentence into words, then maintain both a character-to-word map and a word-to-character map. Every new aligned pair must agree with any previous mapping on both sides.

## Key Insight

Checking only one direction misses the case where two different pattern characters map to the same word. The reverse map enforces the injective part of the bijection.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
solutions.code: class Solution { public boolean wordPattern(String pattern, String s) { String[] words = s.split(" "); if (words.length != pattern.length()) return false; java.util.Map<Character,String> charToWord = new java.util.HashMap<>(); java.util.Map<String,Character> wordToChar = new java.util.HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++) { char ch = pattern.charAt(i); String word = words[i]; if (charToWord.containsKey(ch) && !charToWord.get(ch).equals(word)) return false; if (wordToChar.containsKey(word) && wordToChar.get(word) != ch) return false; charToWord.put(ch, word); wordToChar.put(word, ch); } return true; } }

solutions.name: Mapping with Used Word Set
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use one map from pattern character to word and a set of words that are already assigned. When a character is new, reject the pair if its word is already used by a different character.

## Key Insight

The set carries the same information as a reverse map, but it separates the two responsibilities: the map checks consistency for repeated characters, and the set prevents two characters from sharing one word.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
solutions.code: class Solution { public boolean wordPattern(String pattern, String s) { String[] words = s.split(" "); if (words.length != pattern.length()) return false; java.util.Map<Character,String> mapping = new java.util.HashMap<>(); java.util.Set<String> usedWords = new java.util.HashSet<>(); for (int i = 0; i < pattern.length(); i++) { char ch = pattern.charAt(i); String word = words[i]; if (mapping.containsKey(ch)) { if (!mapping.get(ch).equals(word)) return false; } else { if (usedWords.contains(word)) return false; mapping.put(ch, word); usedWords.add(word); } } return true; } }

solutions.name: Encoded First Positions
solutions.description:
## Approach

Encode both aligned sequences by first occurrence index. At each position, the pattern character and word must have appeared first at the same earlier index, or both must be new.

## Key Insight

A bijection is exactly equality of first-occurrence signatures. For example, `abba` and `dog cat cat dog` both encode as `0,1,1,0`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
solutions.code: class Solution { public boolean wordPattern(String pattern, String s) { String[] words = s.split(" "); if (words.length != pattern.length()) return false; java.util.Map<Object,Integer> first = new java.util.HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++) { Integer patternFirst = first.putIfAbsent(pattern.charAt(i), i); Integer wordFirst = first.putIfAbsent(words[i], i); if (!java.util.Objects.equals(patternFirst, wordFirst)) return false; } return true; } }

solutions.name: Unique Pair Cardinality
solutions.description:
## Approach

After confirming that the lengths match, count unique pattern characters, unique words, and unique `(character, word)` pairs. The mapping is bijective only when all three counts are equal.

## Key Insight

If one character maps to two words, the pair count grows beyond the character count. If two characters map to one word, the character count grows beyond the word count. Equal counts rule out both failure modes.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
solutions.code: class Solution { public boolean wordPattern(String pattern, String s) { String[] words = s.split(" "); if (words.length != pattern.length()) return false; java.util.Set<Character> chars = new java.util.HashSet<>(); java.util.Set<String> seenWords = new java.util.HashSet<>(); java.util.Set<String> pairs = new java.util.HashSet<>(); for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++) { char ch = pattern.charAt(i); chars.add(ch); seenWords.add(words[i]); pairs.add(ch + "\u0001" + words[i]); } return chars.size() == seenWords.size() && chars.size() == pairs.size(); } }
